extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and practitioners of lyric poetry (especially Horatian/classical poets); creative writers seeking Horatian principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit principles for composing Latin lyric (Horatian-style) odes: selecting suitable subjects, choosing appropriate measures and tone, striving for originality, and adopting the necessary versatility of voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate subject-to-genre matching
rubrics_metrics.description: “let therefore the muse that presides over severe tragedy, be for a while absent from the theaters; shortly, when thou hast completed the narrative of the public affairs, you shall resume your great work in the tragic style of Athens, O Pollio... do not insist that the long wars of fierce Numantia, or the formidable Annibal... should be adapted to the tender lays of the lyre: nor the cruel Lapithae...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects suited to the poetic mode: do not force grand, long, or historiographic subjects (wars, prolonged national crises) into intimate lyric forms. Reserve epic/historical treatment for prose or more elevated tragic/epic genres; use lyric measures for private, amorous, or lighter themes. (Example guidance in the text: "rather with me seek measures of a lighter style beneath some love-sequestered grotto.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metrical measures and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: “seek measures of a lighter style beneath some love-sequestered grotto.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match meter and rhythmic 'measures' to subject-matter and mood: light, graceful meters for love and convivial themes; more severe measures for weighty, tragic material. The poet should deliberately select the musical qualities of verse to suit content and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality — "verses not heard before"
rubrics_metrics.description: “Preserve a religious silence: I, the priest of the Muses, sing to virgins and boys verses not heard before.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for freshness in theme, phrasing, and imagery rather than repeating commonplaces. Horace presents the poet as an initiatory figure who brings new songs to a specific audience: value novelty and avoid hackneyed tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility of poetic persona (“two-formed” poet)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I, a two-formed poet, will be conveyed through the liquid air with no vulgar or humble wing... Now, a melodious bird... I will visit the shores... Let there be no dirges, nor unmanly lamentations...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the capacity to adopt different poetic modes and voices (light and playful, grave and elevated). The poet should be able to change tone, subject, and register as occasion demands rather than be confined to a single mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit invocations and dedications to occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: “What does the poet beg from Phoebus on the dedication of his temple?... Not the rich crops of fertile Sardinia... Me olives support... O thou son of Latona, grant me to enjoy my acquisitions, and to possess my health, together with an unimpaired understanding...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing dedications or invocations, tailor petitions and language to the ritual/occasion and to modest, fitting aims. Horace contrasts extravagant material petitions with modest, personal requests (health, contentment, artistic preservation) as appropriate subject matter for a lyric invocation.
